title: Earth’s atmosphere loses free oxygen
shortDescription: Earth’s atmosphere will lose almost all free oxygen, making complex life impossible — in about 1 billion years.
mainDescription: Earth’s atmosphere is expected to undergo a profound transformation roughly one billion years in the future as the Sun gradually becomes brighter and more energetic. Over time, increasing solar luminosity will warm the planet enough to accelerate the evaporation of Earth’s oceans. As water vapor rises into the upper atmosphere, ultraviolet radiation from the Sun will break apart water molecules, allowing hydrogen to escape into space. Without stable oceans and active photosynthetic life, atmospheric oxygen levels are expected to decline dramatically. Eventually, Earth may lose most of its free oxygen, transforming the atmosphere into one far less hospitable to complex aerobic organisms. Long before the Sun reaches its final stages of evolution, the planet’s surface could already become largely uninhabitable for the forms of life familiar today. The transition illustrates that planetary habitability is not permanent, but part of a long evolutionary cycle shaped by the changing energy output of stars.
whatYoullSee: A planet with a thin, oxygen-depleted atmosphere and dying biosphere.
whyItMatters: The final decline of complex multicellular life on Earth.
nextOccurrences: Complex life will not recover after this point.

title: The death of Earth – runaway greenhouse
shortDescription: Earth becomes a lifeless Venus-like planet as oceans boil away — in about 2 billion years.
mainDescription: Earth is expected to become uninhabitable in roughly two billion years as the Sun continues its slow increase in brightness. As solar energy reaching Earth rises over immense timescales, the planet’s climate may eventually cross a critical threshold known as a runaway greenhouse state. Increasing temperatures would cause the oceans to evaporate rapidly, filling the atmosphere with large amounts of water vapor — itself a powerful greenhouse gas that would trap even more heat. Over time, Earth’s oceans could disappear completely, leaving behind a hot, dry surface beneath a dense and hostile atmosphere. Temperatures may climb high enough to sterilize much of the planet, ending the long era during which Earth supported complex life. The transformation would resemble, in some ways, the extreme greenhouse conditions seen on present-day Venus. Long before the Sun reaches the end of its life, Earth itself may already become a barren world shaped by the evolving power of its parent star.
whatYoullSee: A barren, red-hot planet with no liquid water and a dense, oppressive atmosphere.
whyItMatters: This is the final end of Earth as a habitable planet — the death of our home world.
nextOccurrences: Earth will never recover habitability after this event.

title: First signs of Milky Way and Andromeda interaction
shortDescription: The first gravitational distortions between the Milky Way and Andromeda become noticeable — in about 3 billion years.
mainDescription: The first visible signs of the future collision between the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy are expected to emerge roughly three billion years from now. As Andromeda continues moving toward the Milky Way at hundreds of kilometers per second, its gravitational influence will gradually begin to distort the outer regions of both galaxies. Long streams of stars and gas may form along their edges, while the structure of the night sky slowly changes over millions of years. By this stage, Andromeda would appear far larger and brighter in Earth’s sky than it does today, stretching across a significant portion of the heavens. The once distant spiral galaxy visible to modern observers as a faint patch of light would become an enormous and increasingly dominant object overhead. Although the galaxies contain hundreds of billions of stars, direct stellar collisions are expected to remain extremely rare because of the immense distances between stars. Instead, the interaction will primarily reshape both galaxies through gravity, beginning one of the largest transformations in the future history of the Local Group.
whatYoullSee: Subtle but growing changes in the structure and star density of our galaxy’s outskirts.
whyItMatters: The beginning of the greatest galactic event in our cosmic neighborhood.
keyFacts: Leads to the formation of Milkomeda
nextOccurrences: The full merger will occur around 4.5 billion years from now.

title: Milky Way collides with Andromeda
shortDescription: Our galaxy merges with Andromeda forming a giant elliptical galaxy — in about 4.5 billion years.
mainDescription: The Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy are expected to collide and begin merging roughly 4 to 5 billion years from now, reshaping the future of the Local Group of galaxies. As the two giant spiral galaxies pass through one another, their structures will become severely distorted by gravity. Vast streams of stars, gas, and dust will be pulled across intergalactic space while intense waves of star formation ignite throughout the merging system. Over hundreds of millions of years, the separate galaxies will gradually lose their familiar spiral shapes and combine into a single much larger galaxy often nicknamed “Milkomeda.” From the perspective of any future observers within the Milky Way, the night sky would change dramatically. Andromeda would eventually dominate the heavens, growing larger over time until the two galaxies overlap across enormous portions of the sky. Despite the scale of the collision, direct impacts between stars are expected to remain extremely unlikely because stars are separated by immense distances. Instead, the merger will primarily unfold as a slow gravitational transformation affecting billions of stars across millions of light-years.
whatYoullSee: The night sky filled with millions of bright new stars and completely reshaped galactic structure.
whyItMatters: The greatest galactic event in our local universe for billions of years.
keyFacts: Two largest galaxies in the Local Group
nextOccurrences: The merged galaxy will stabilize over billions of years.

title: The Sun engulfs Earth – red giant phase
shortDescription: The Sun expands into a red giant and destroys Earth — in about 7.6 billion years.
mainDescription: The Sun is expected to enter its red giant phase roughly 7 to 8 billion years from now, transforming the inner Solar System beyond recognition. As hydrogen fuel in the Sun’s core becomes depleted, the star will begin expanding outward to enormous dimensions. Over time, the Sun’s outer layers may extend beyond the present orbits of Mercury and Venus, while Earth’s surface temperatures rise far beyond anything compatible with liquid water or life. Whether Earth is completely engulfed or survives briefly in a scorched orbit remains uncertain, but the planet would almost certainly become a molten and lifeless world long before the final stages of the expansion. Oceans, atmosphere, and surface geology would disappear beneath the intense heat of the evolving star. From the outer Solar System, the future Sun would appear vastly larger and redder than today, dominating the sky as one of the final major phases in the life cycle of our star. The event marks the beginning of the end for the planetary system that has existed around the Sun for billions of years.
whatYoullSee: The Sun growing monstrously large until it fills the sky and consumes our planet.
whyItMatters: The physical destruction of Earth by its own star.
keyFacts: Sun expands over 200 times its current size
nextOccurrences: The Sun will then evolve into a white dwarf.

title: The Sun becomes a white dwarf
shortDescription: The Sun dies and shrinks into a cold white dwarf — in about 10 billion years.
mainDescription: After exhausting its remaining nuclear fuel, the Sun will cast off its outer layers and collapse into a white dwarf — the final stable stage in the life of a star like ours. During this transformation, the Sun will create a glowing planetary nebula as expanding shells of gas drift outward into space. At the center, the former core of the Sun will remain as an extremely dense white dwarf roughly comparable in size to Earth, yet containing a large fraction of the Sun’s original mass. Without active nuclear fusion, the white dwarf will no longer generate significant new energy. Instead, it will slowly radiate away its remaining heat over trillions of years, gradually fading and cooling as the surrounding Solar System grows dark and cold. Any surviving planets, moons, or remnants of the Solar System would continue orbiting the stellar remnant in near-total darkness, illuminated only by the faint residual glow of the dying star and the distant light of other stars in the galaxy.
whatYoullSee: A faint, dying ember where our once brilliant Sun used to shine.
whyItMatters: The final death of our star.
nextOccurrences: The white dwarf will continue cooling for trillions of years.

title: End of all star formation
shortDescription: No new stars will ever form again — in about 1 trillion years.
mainDescription: The universe is expected to gradually run out of the cold gas needed to create new stars, bringing the long Stelliferous Era — the age of stars — to an end. Over immense stretches of cosmic time, galaxies continuously consume their reservoirs of hydrogen and other star-forming material. Some gas is locked away inside stars, planets, stellar remnants, and black holes, while the remaining supply becomes increasingly diffuse and difficult to compress into new generations of stars. Eventually, star formation across the universe will slow to a near halt. The bright blue stars common in younger galaxies will disappear, leaving behind mostly long-lived red dwarfs, white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. Galaxies themselves will become darker, quieter, and far less active than they are today. The end of star formation marks a profound transition in cosmic history: the universe will continue to exist, but the era dominated by shining stars and luminous galaxies will slowly fade into a colder and dimmer future.
whatYoullSee: The universe growing darker as the last generations of stars begin to die.
whyItMatters: The end of the luminous, star-filled chapter of cosmic history.
keyFacts: All hydrogen for star formation depleted
nextOccurrences: The universe enters the Degenerate Era.

title: The last star in the universe dies
shortDescription: The final star burns out, plunging the universe into eternal darkness — in about 100 trillion years.
mainDescription: The final stars in the universe are expected to fade away roughly 100 trillion years in the future, bringing an end to the last remaining sources of natural starlight. By this era, nearly all large and medium-sized stars will have long since disappeared, leaving only extremely long-lived red dwarfs still capable of nuclear fusion. These small stars burn their fuel extraordinarily slowly, allowing some to survive for tens to hundreds of trillions of years — far longer than stars like the Sun. Eventually, even the last red dwarfs will exhaust their hydrogen and cool into dark stellar remnants. After the final star goes dark, the universe will enter an age without new sunlight, sunsets, or naturally illuminated skies. Galaxies that once blazed with billions of stars will become dominated by faint remnants, black holes, and slowly cooling matter. The death of the last star marks the end of the Stelliferous Era — the final chapter in the age of luminous stars that began shortly after the birth of the universe.
whatYoullSee: Complete cosmic darkness. No stars, only faint remnants of dead stellar objects.
whyItMatters: The definitive end of light in the observable universe.
nextOccurrences: The universe enters the Black Hole Era.

title: Proton decay – the dissolution of matter
shortDescription: All ordinary matter begins to decay — in ~10³⁴ years.
mainDescription: If protons are ultimately unstable, the universe may enter an era in which matter itself slowly disappears. Many theories in particle physics suggest that protons — one of the fundamental building blocks of atoms — may not last forever, even though no proton decay has ever been observed. Over unimaginable stretches of time, isolated protons could gradually decay into lighter particles and radiation, causing ordinary matter to break apart atom by atom. If proton decay occurs, planets, white dwarfs, neutron stars, and nearly all remaining structures made of normal matter would slowly dissolve. Solid objects would cease to exist, leaving behind an increasingly diffuse universe filled mostly with radiation, elementary particles, and black holes. The process would unfold across timescales so vast that they dwarf the entire current age of the universe by many orders of magnitude. It represents one possible final transition from a universe filled with matter to one approaching near-total physical darkness and decay.
whatYoullSee: Even the densest remnants of stars gradually fade into light and elementary particles.
whyItMatters: The end of ordinary matter itself.
nextOccurrences: Only black holes and elementary particles remain.

title: The black hole era
shortDescription: Black holes become the only significant objects left in the universe.
mainDescription: After the disappearance of most ordinary matter, the universe may enter the Black Hole Era — a period when black holes become the dominant remaining structures in the cosmos. By this stage, stars, planets, and galaxies as they exist today will largely be gone. If proton decay occurs, even the remnants of dead stars and scattered matter will gradually dissolve, leaving black holes as some of the last surviving large-scale objects in the universe. Although black holes are often imagined as eternal, quantum effects predicted by Stephen Hawking suggest that they slowly lose energy through a process known as Hawking radiation. Over extraordinarily long timescales, even supermassive black holes containing billions of solar masses would begin to evaporate particle by particle. The process is unimaginably slow. The largest black holes could survive for periods vastly longer than the current age of the universe before finally fading away in faint bursts of radiation. During this era, the cosmos would become increasingly dark, cold, and empty, with isolated black holes slowly disappearing across near-infinite stretches of time.
whatYoullSee: A nearly empty universe containing only isolated supermassive black holes.
whyItMatters: The longest single era in the future history of the universe.
nextOccurrences: All black holes will eventually evaporate.

title: All black holes evaporate
shortDescription: Even the last black holes disappear — in ~10¹⁰⁰ years.
mainDescription: Even black holes — among the longest-lived objects in the universe — are expected to eventually disappear. According to Hawking radiation theory, black holes slowly lose energy through quantum effects near their event horizons. Over immense stretches of time, this gradual energy loss causes them to shrink and slowly evaporate particle by particle. For stellar-mass black holes the process is extraordinarily slow, while supermassive black holes may survive for timescales vastly exceeding the current age of the universe. As evaporation accelerates near the end of a black hole’s existence, the remaining mass would be released in bursts of high-energy radiation and particles. After the final black holes vanish, no compact objects capable of shaping galaxies or trapping light would remain anywhere in the cosmos. The evaporation of the last black holes represents one of the final major transitions in many models of the far future universe — a stage where even the darkest and most massive structures ultimately fade away.
whatYoullSee: The final sources of structure and energy in the universe flickering out.
whyItMatters: The end of the last macroscopic objects in the cosmos.
nextOccurrences: Only a dilute sea of particles remains.

title: Heat death of the universe – the final end
shortDescription: The universe reaches maximum entropy and dies in eternal cold and darkness.
mainDescription: The universe may eventually approach a state known as heat death — a future in which nearly all physical processes come to an end. Over incomprehensibly vast stretches of time, stars will burn out, galaxies will fade, matter may decay, and even black holes could evaporate. As the universe continues expanding, energy becomes increasingly diluted across space, while temperatures everywhere move closer to absolute uniformity. In this final state, no significant energy gradients would remain to power stars, chemistry, motion, or complex structures. The cosmos would become extraordinarily dark, cold, and diffuse, populated only by sparse particles and faint low-energy radiation spread across an ever-expanding universe. Heat death does not describe a sudden catastrophe, but rather an endless fading of activity itself — a universe approaching maximum entropy, where time continues, yet almost nothing meaningful can still occur.
whatYoullSee: Absolute void. No light, no heat, no motion — the complete end of everything.
whyItMatters: The ultimate fate of the universe: the final, irreversible end of all existence.
